title: Birthday draft lottery
materials: Birthday slips: every boy’s, plus 20–30 family birthdays collected ahead of time
Whiteboard with a blank draft-eras table

displayContent.headline: The birthday draw
displayContent.body: Every birthday is in an egg. We’ll draw them one at a time and post the order.

prompts.text: Why would anyone draw birthdays out of a bucket?
prompts.answer: On December 1, 1969, the Selective Service did exactly this, live on TV, with every day of the year. Men born 1944–1950 got a number by birthday, and low numbers were called first.

prompts.text: Was letting a man pay $300 to stay home fair? Who could afford it?
prompts.answer: Let them argue. Anger over the rule helped spark the New York City draft riots in July 1863.

prompts.text: Is a lottery fairer than letting local boards choose? Why or why not?
prompts.answer: No single right answer. The 1969 lottery replaced choosing with chance: your birthday decided your number.

prompts.text: For the Adventurers: what does the law ask of you at 18?
prompts.answer: Men 18 through 25 must be registered with the Selective Service, and from December 2026 registration becomes automatic. Registering isn’t being drafted; nobody has been drafted since 1973.

leaderScript: Draw the eggs one at a time and post the order on the board.
Press → for the first question, R for the answer.
Press → for the draft-eras table. Fill in the board together first, then press R to check.
Keep question 4 factual: registration is the law; a draft would be a separate decision. Stay off current politics.

discussionQuestions.question: What is conscription?
discussionQuestions.answer: The draft: the law requiring people to serve, usually in the military.

cells: Could hire a substitute or pay $300 to avoid service
About 24 million registered; about 2.8 million drafted
Selective Training and Service Act of 1940

ifShortOnTime: Draw only the boys’ birthdays, show the eras table already filled in, and ask just question 4.
